subject: Computer Networking
title: Network Attached Storage (NAS)
description: A fast breakdown of Network Attached Storage (NAS) for builders.

hook.text: A NAS is a dedicated storage box on your network. Any authorized device can read and write to it.

buildup.text: NAS devices use multiple drives in RAID arrays. RAID provides speed, redundancy, or both.

discovery.text: SMB and NFS let computers mount NAS drives as if they were local. File sharing becomes seamless.

twist.text: Enterprise NAS from NetApp and Synology can store petabytes with snapshots, replication, and encryption.

climax.text: For home users, a NAS replaces cloud storage. Your files, your network, no monthly fees.

punchline.text: A NAS puts shared storage on your network. Your own cloud.

quiz.question: What does RAID provide in a NAS device?
options: Data redundancy, speed improvement, or both
Automatic virus scanning of stored files

details.summary: A NAS device is a dedicated file storage appliance connected to the network, allowing multiple users and devices to access shared files over standard protocols like SMB and NFS. NAS devices range from simple two-bay home units to enterprise rackmount systems with dozens of drives.
details.whyItMatters: NAS centralizes file storage, eliminating scattered copies across individual devices. Understanding NAS helps teams share files efficiently and maintain reliable backups.
takeaways: NAS provides centralized file storage accessible over the network
RAID configurations protect data against drive failures
Modern NAS devices support apps for backup, media, and Docker

faq.question: What is the difference between NAS and a regular external drive?
faq.answer: An external drive connects to one computer via USB. A NAS connects to the network and serves files to every authorized device simultaneously. NAS devices run their own operating system, support user permissions, RAID for redundancy, and remote access from anywhere.

faq.question: How does RAID protect data on a NAS?
faq.answer: RAID mirrors or distributes data across multiple drives so that one or more drives can fail without data loss. RAID 1 mirrors two drives. RAID 5 stripes data with parity across three or more drives, tolerating one drive failure. RAID 6 tolerates two simultaneous failures.
